title: Customer security questionnaires answered from an approved knowledge base
problem: Customer security reviews arrive as long forms answered by hand from policies and audit reports, so a small GRC team becomes a sales bottleneck.
approach: Answers are drafted from approved company documents; only low-confidence or unmatched questions go to an analyst.
GitHub reports automating 93% of inbound questionnaires in 6 months, against a 12-month goal (vendor-published).
Carta reports an 83% decrease in review time and 95% AI accuracy (vendor-published); how accuracy was judged is not stated.

title: Self-serve trust centre with an AI agent answering security questions
problem: Customers repeatedly request the same audit reports and policies, then ask follow-up questions the documents already answer, which Sumo Logic's compliance lead likens to a second full-time job.
approach: A trust centre exposes audit reports and policies with automated NDA rules, and an AI agent answers inbound questions from that content.
Questions the agent cannot answer, and non-standard requests, still reach the security team.
Synthesia reports 20-30% of customer questions resolved without staff and sales cycles two weeks shorter (vendor-published).

title: Agent-drafted vendor security assessments, with an analyst deciding residual risk
problem: Each new vendor's SOC 2 report, pen test summary and questionnaire must be read against the buyer's standards; volume outgrows analysts and reviews take weeks.
approach: An AI agent collects vendor documents, extracts exceptions and risk signals, drafts an evaluation and prepares follow-up questions.
An analyst verifies the draft and decides inherent and residual risk; customers can choose between autonomous and in-the-loop operation.
Samsara reports vendor reviews up to 50% faster (vendor-published); a payments company reports 150 assessments in under 2 weeks (vendor-published).

title: Continuous vendor monitoring with reassessment when something changes
problem: Vendor approvals are point-in-time, so new reports, subprocessors, incidents or AI features added after approval can change risk without anyone reopening the review.
approach: The programme defines triggers such as a new SOC 2 report, subprocessor or vendor incident, on which an analyst reopens the assessment.
Vendors including Safe and Vanta sell agents that monitor breaches, contracts and vendor changes; no outcome figures are published.
Idea: extend the inventory to vendor-embedded agents, with a named human reviewer for AI-generated findings that trigger action.

title: Mapping and rationalising controls and evidence across frameworks with an agent
problem: Organisations holding many frameworks keep duplicate controls and map evidence by hand; Synthesia's case study puts matching 500+ HITRUST controls at 1.5 months of manual work.
approach: An agent proposes a common control framework and maps controls and evidence to each framework; a GRC owner approves the mapping.
Samsara reports consolidating 820 controls to 260 (68% reduction) across 10 frameworks (vendor-published).
Synthesia reports HITRUST implementation compressed from 18 months to about 3 months (vendor-published).

title: Agent-run evidence collection and continuous control monitoring
problem: Control evidence is gathered by hand before each audit, so failures surface late; manual compliance work took up to 60% of Perforce's team time.
approach: Connectors pull evidence from source systems; agents check it against control descriptions, flag drift and send issues to control owners.
Control owners drive findings to closure, and humans own thresholds and policy; external audit cycles continue.
Perforce reports compliance work falling from 60% to 15% of team time; Synthesia reports 60% of evidence collection automated (vendor-published).

title: Agents test controls end to end and assemble audit workpapers for review
problem: Control testing is done by sampling and manual fieldwork, then written up as workpapers for internal and external auditors.
approach: Agents ingest unstructured evidence, run attribute tests on the full set of uploaded evidence and record each step.
They assemble Excel workpapers linked to source evidence; auditors review the workpapers and exceptions.
Optro announced this capability; no outcome figures are published.

title: Drafting and keeping security policies current with AI
problem: Policy sets must be written and updated for each new framework, and generic chatbot requests for a security policy produce generic output.
approach: AI drafts tailored policy documents and keeps a policy database current across frameworks.
Prompt templates supply audience, tech stack, certifications and current state; the policy owner reviews and approves drafts.
Synthesia reports its policy database kept current across six frameworks (vendor-published); an independent test of policy-to-code translation reports 50.3% vs 15.3% (independent).

title: Gap analysis of security policies against a standard and actual practice
problem: Security policies are often incomplete against standards and drift from what teams do; finding gaps takes extensive manual effort and scarce experienced reviewers.
approach: AI compares policies with programme data or customer-facing reports and surfaces inconsistencies for policy owners to fix.
In a lab benchmark, small open-weight models judged ISO 27002 controls as met or not met, as an assistant to the auditor.
Best model's mean agreement with the human expert was 80.65% (independent); four of eight models reached 52.4-59.9% balanced accuracy.

title: Mapping AI and security regulations into policy and controls
problem: A Gartner analyst describes the AI regulatory landscape as fragmented and volatile, and teams must keep policy-to-regulation mappings current.
approach: Governance engineers use AI-assisted workflows to monitor regulations, assess impact with Legal and update policy mappings.
Gartner advises building a baseline on shared principles rather than law-by-law compliance, with cross-functional review of which mandates apply.
No outcome figures are published.

title: Risk register upkeep, intake triage and first-draft risk analyses with AI
problem: Risk intake, register upkeep, first-draft analyses and reporting are manual work; Anthropic and Plaid job postings seek AI-based automation of it.
approach: Anthropic plans Claude-based tooling to classify and triage incoming risks; Plaid seeks automations for first-draft analyses and reports.
Analysts own calibration and quality review of AI outputs.
An independent comparison of five LLMs with 50 human experts found LLM risk scores consistently lower.

title: Cyber risk quantification with AI: data gathering and expert elicitation
problem: Structured expert elicitation produces calibrated estimates but takes months of coordination, while boards ask for decision-ready, data-driven numbers.
approach: Anthropic plans Claude-based tooling to sense changes in the risk landscape; researchers use LLM personas to replace or supplement expert panels.
Analysts own estimate calibration; 89% of survey respondents have board-approved risk thresholds.
A lab study reports Pearson r = 0.91-0.98 against ground truth (independent); T-Mobile reports a 75% reduction in reporting time (vendor-published).

title: Risk analysis extended to the organisation's own AI agents and model providers
problem: Analysts must assess software agents that hold privileges and can bind the company, but the FAIR threat taxonomy defines AI agents only as malicious tools.
approach: The FAIR Institute's standards director proposes treating agents as privileged insiders and model providers as third parties.
Analysts collect three numbers on agent activity: share reviewed, delay, and how often review catches something.
Human approval is required for agent actions above a defined threshold; no outcome figures are published.
who: FAIR Institute, PwC, UC Berkeley CLTC

title: Board and executive risk reports drafted from programme data
problem: Gartner analysts say many board reports are built around cybersecurity rather than the business, and CISOs may get only five to ten minutes with the board.
approach: Idea: programme data feeds a board pack that AI drafts and the CISO edits; no source describes this in use.
Perforce plans to use its GRC platform for regular risk reviews and board-level reporting.
The CISO owns the narrative and the requests to the board; no outcome figures are published.

title: Audit response drafting and consolidating several audits around one evidence set
problem: Each external audit asks subject experts for the same walkthroughs and evidence, and several audits run in parallel.
approach: AI drafts responses to auditor requests from existing evidence, and one evidence set is mapped to several frameworks.
No source describes who reviews AI-drafted audit responses; under NIS2 a named executive owns what is filed.
Synthesia reports five framework audit cycles in one month; Samsara reports expert time per cycle falling from 70 to 40 hours (vendor-published).

title: Verifying automated compliance evidence and auditor independence
problem: After a whistleblower alleged the platform Delve generated fabricated SOC 2 and ISO 27001 evidence (the company denies this), practitioners worry that customers relying on the certificates carry the liability.
approach: IANS faculty advise buyers to re-read their SOC 2 report and ask the platform vendor what the auditor can access.
Buyers get written confirmation that the auditor designed its own tests and spot-check 5 to 10 controls at random.
No outcome figures are published.

title: Security team writes AI policy and approval gates for tools and agents
problem: Staff adopt AI tools and agents faster than policy; security teams must decide what data agents may touch and which actions need human approval.
approach: GRC writes agent governance policies, sets approval criteria and sits as reviewer in engineering approval workflows.
Cengage reports assessing 67 AI vendors in 15 months (self-reported), aiming not to be 'the Department of No'.
Sendbird's CISO describes tiered AI tools, blocks on some models and contract review so vendors do not train on customer data.

title: The security team's own AI-use policy: approved tools, logging and autonomy limits
problem: AI is in security work faster than control over it: SANS reports 79% of SOCs use AI or ML tools but only 36% have built them into a defined workflow.
approach: The policy sets approved tools and data classes, an owner for each use, and logging of prompts, outputs and model versions.
Agents get no broad access; deterministic gates and a kill switch outside the agent's control sit before high-risk actions.
Trail of Bits wrote an AI handbook listing approved and unapproved tools; Centene describes hash-verified records of each AI-assisted step.
who: Trail of Bits, Centene, FINRA, SANS

title: GRC engineering team builds compliance automation and agent workflows
problem: Compliance headcount scales with frameworks, vendors and customer requests, yet GRC still runs on spreadsheets and skills are uneven.
approach: GRC teams hire automation engineers, define controls as machine-readable code and expect analysts to build their own AI automations.
The GRC practitioner decides whether a configuration is in fact their control; Anthropic's postings state a human-in-the-loop design.
Anthropic, Figma, Plaid and Cloudflare are hiring for these roles; no outcome figures are published.

title: Security roles redesigned around AI oversight, with role-based AI training
problem: Teams report skills rather than headcount as the binding constraint, and only 20% provide comprehensive AI training for all staff.
approach: Work is reassigned between people and AI; new roles such as AI security engineer and AI governance analyst appear.
Staff get role-based training in AI tools, LLM SecOps (running and securing LLM systems) and AI regulation.
Surveys report 34% creating AI/ML specialist roles and 41% naming AI the most pressing skills need (independent).

title: Deliberate apprenticeship for junior risk staff when AI absorbs entry-level work
problem: Idea, not a deployment: juniors learned what normal looks like from routine work that AI now automates, so Venables argues the talent pipeline fractures within a few years.
approach: Idea: put juniors on control-failure post-mortems instead of evidence gathering, with AI as a coach.
Venables also proposes pod or master-and-apprentice structures and hiring tests that spot errors in AI output.
Juniors review machine-generated work against a standard; no results are published.
